analysis.title: Grow up & Glow Up: How Allocators Should Approach Digital Assets at the Dawn of Their Institutional Era
key_insights: Bitcoin's return distribution has compressed. Annualized daily volatility fell from about 84% in 2017-2019 to about 46% since mid-2024, and the average loss on the worst 5% of days halved from -9.9% to -5.0%. The current era still includes a 53% peak-to-trough decline.

Bitcoin's correlation to traditional assets has retreated from 2022-2024 highs but depends on the equity regime. Correlation to global equities is about 0.4-0.5 when equities are in a negative regime (since 2020) and 0.1-0.3 when equities are strong.

In a diversified institutional portfolio (45% global equity, 25% US bonds, 12% private equity, 10% real estate, 8% hedge funds), a 7.5% bitcoin allocation funded pro rata contributes 20% of total portfolio risk. Franklin's 20% single-position risk guideline therefore implies 7.5% today.

In a 60/40 portfolio, 3% bitcoin contributed 11.4% of risk in the 2025 paper and contributes 6.5% today. A 4% allocation now contributes 9.6% and 6% contributes 16.6%, so an allocation one-third larger carries less risk than the 2025 example did.

Across 12 macro and crypto-specific shocks since 2020, bitcoin's first-week behavior was mixed and its 60-day recovery was stronger than equities' in all six macro episodes. In COVID-19, the one true liquidity shock, bitcoin fell twice as far as equities in week one (-32.1% vs -14.9%) and its equity correlation doubled.

In the 2023 banking crisis, the 2025 tariff shock and the 2026 US-Iran conflict, bitcoin outperformed equities in the first week and over 60 days. The direction of the correlation change tracks the nature of the shock, which Franklin says lets allocators make dynamic allocation decisions from macro forecasts.

Bitcoin's share of portfolio risk rises faster than its weight. In the institutional portfolio, 2% of capital is 3.8% of risk, 6% is 15.0%, 10% is 28.4%. Volatility rises 0.1 percentage points at 2% and 0.7 points at 6%.

Rolling risk contribution is time-varying. A 10% allocation contributed 90-95% of portfolio risk in 2017-2018, 75-80% in 2021 and 40-45% in 2024-2025, and about 25% at June 2026. Franklin recommends risk-contribution ceilings (it uses 20%) as rebalancing triggers, reviewed at least quarterly, with symmetric adding back when risk share falls well below target.

De-smoothed private equity carries roughly a fifth of the institutional portfolio's ex-ante risk at a 12% weight, more than a 10% bitcoin allocation does. Franklin says real estate and hedge fund series are used as reported and likely understate risk.

Franklin advises funding digital assets from the highest-volatility or fattest-tail sleeves such as emerging market equities and high yield, and offsetting part of the added risk with US Treasuries. Funding from public equities alone gives near-identical risk shares (15.3% at 6%).

Crypto-specific milestones moved bitcoin without moving equities, and correlations afterward were typically low. The ETF approval and the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve were followed by short-term reversals.

Franklin Templeton Digital Assets runs a systematic ether trend-following strategy with a regime-aware machine-learning overlay. Since October 2022 its monthly correlation is 0.61 with spot bitcoin, 0.18 with global equities and -0.03 with US aggregate bonds. The paper suggests replacing a fifth of a spot-bitcoin sleeve with it.
crypto_views: Bitcoin is considered a long-duration, high-volatility asset with moderate, time-varying equity beta, and the paper treats cryptocurrencies as a fundamentally new asset class. It rejects the 'digital gold' framing because the precious metals relationship has never been persistent.

Franklin attributes lower volatility to institutional participation (spot ETFs, corporate treasuries, staked and long-term holdings) that centralizes holdings with long-term holders who trade less. It says it cannot attribute the improvement exclusively to adoption and makes no return projection.

Bitcoin correlations on the recent-weighted covariance: 0.32 with global equities, -0.01 with aggregate bonds, 0.28 with private equity, 0.22 with real estate, 0.18 with hedge funds. Private equity and hedge funds correlate 0.72 and 0.84 with global equities.
The 2022 drawdown, driven by crypto-native leverage rather than macro, was 7% deeper than the era before it.
Bitcoin's 36-month rolling correlation to commodities fell to about -0.2, and to US high yield to about 0.1-0.2.

trade_ideas.description: Allocate to bitcoin as a benchmark position at about 7.5% in a diversified institutional portfolio (20% risk contribution ceiling), funded pro rata or from the highest-volatility sleeves such as EM equities and high yield
trade_ideas.rationale: Lower volatility and correlation mean the same 20% risk ceiling now accommodates a larger weight than in 2025.
trade_ideas.risk: Bitcoin remains prone to large drawdowns, with a 53% peak-to-trough decline in the current era, and a high-beta asset in a true liquidity shock.

trade_ideas.description: Replace a fifth of a spot-bitcoin sleeve with Franklin's systematic ether trend-following strategy
trade_ideas.rationale: The strategy reduces the sleeve's dependence on bitcoin-specific directional risk, with a 0.61 correlation to spot bitcoin.
trade_ideas.risk: Only 45 months of live history, too short to support tail-risk estimates with confidence.

risk_factors: Bitcoin remains a high-beta asset in a true liquidity shock, and its drawdowns are still measured in halves.
Bitcoin's risk contribution swings by a factor of several within a cycle, and even a 4% allocation has reached roughly 40-50% of portfolio risk in the worst episodes.
Bitcoin-equity correlation rises in negative equity regimes, so diversification is weakest in sell-offs.
Smoothed private and alternative valuations understate risk, and public and private marks diverged for several quarters in 2022.
Anticipated catalysts are priced before they arrive, and several crypto milestones were followed by short-term reversals.
Past performance is not a guide to future returns, and the paper makes no return projection.
charts_described: Exhibit 1: bitcoin rolling 36-month correlation with global equities fell from about 0.5-0.6 to about 0.3, with US high yield at about 0.1-0.2 and commodities at about -0.2.
Exhibit 9: bitcoin share of total portfolio risk for 2%-10% allocations, with peaks falling from about 90% in 2017-2018 to 40-45% in 2024-2025 for the 10% allocation.
vol_and_positioning: Bitcoin 95% daily VaR improved from -7.7% to -4.0% and 95% daily CVaR from -10.3% to -5.3% between the first and current eras.
Excess kurtosis rose from 2.56 to 4.42 across the first two eras and fell to 2.68 in the current era. Skewness is near zero throughout, +0.22 in the current era.

Bitcoin 200-day volatility fell after the 2023 banking crisis (53.0% to 43.3%), the 2025 tariff shock (51.4% to 37.7%) and the 2026 US-Iran conflict (48.0% to 39.1%) while equity volatility rose in the latter two.

Regime framework: global equity regimes are scored from five trend and momentum indicators. Bitcoin-equity correlation is most recently 0.43 in negative regimes and 0.29 in positive regimes. Franklin advises stress testing portfolios for bitcoin behaving like equities in a sell-off.
geopolitical: US-Iran conflict (strikes Saturday Feb 28, 2026): energy-price channel hit traditional assets while bitcoin outperformed equities in week one (+4.2% vs -3.7%) and over 60 days (+16.7% vs +1.5%)
Russia-Ukraine invasion (Feb 24, 2022) became an inflation and rates shock, and bitcoin-equity correlation reached its highest post-event level in the sample

tension_points.bull_case: Bitcoin's volatility has roughly halved, equity correlation has fallen toward 0.3 and correlation with bonds is near zero, so a 7.5% allocation fits within a 20% risk ceiling.
tension_points.bear_case: Bitcoin correlation with equities is 0.4-0.5 in negative equity regimes, it fell twice as far as equities in the COVID liquidity shock, and drawdowns are still measured in halves.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A breach of the 20% risk-contribution ceiling on a rolling basis, which Franklin says should trigger a trim.

theme_stances.key_argument: Lower volatility means the same 20% risk ceiling now accommodates a larger bitcoin allocation, but it should be governed by rolling risk monitoring.
theme_stances.evidence: The same 20% risk ceiling now accommodates a 7.5% allocation.
